subject: science
cluster: Stars, the Sun, and patterns in the sky
skillName: Patterns in Shadows, Day and Night, and Seasons

items.prompt: At what time of day is a shadow usually shortest?

steps: The Sun is highest near noon, so shadows are shortest then.

items.prompt: When is a shadow longest during the day?

steps: The Sun is low in the morning and evening, making shadows long.

items.prompt: What causes the repeating pattern of day and night?
items.answer: The Earth spinning (rotating) once each day

steps: Rotation turns each place toward and away from the Sun.

items.prompt: Do the same stars appear in the night sky in every season?

steps: Different constellations are visible in different seasons.

items.prompt: How often does the seasonal pattern of constellations repeat?

steps: The same seasonal stars return each year as Earth orbits the Sun.

items.prompt: Why is a graph useful for showing shadow data?
items.answer: It makes the pattern easy to see

steps: A graph reveals trends that are hard to spot in a list of numbers.

items.prompt: A shadow points toward the west in the early morning. Does its direction change during the day?

steps: As the Sun appears to move across the sky, the shadow direction changes.

items.prompt: In which direction does the Sun appear to rise?

steps: The Sun appears to rise in the east and set in the west.

items.prompt: A graph of daylight hours is short in winter and long in summer. What repeats this pattern?
items.answer: Earth's yearly orbit around the Sun

steps: Daylight length changes through the seasons and repeats each year.

items.prompt: Describe the shape of a graph of shadow length from morning to evening.
items.answer: It starts high, drops to a lowest point near noon, then rises again

steps: Shadows start long, shorten to a minimum at noon, then lengthen.

items.prompt: How can a shadow-length graph be used to estimate when noon occurs?
items.answer: Noon is near the time when the shadow is shortest on the graph

steps: The lowest point of the graph marks the time the Sun is highest, near noon.

items.prompt: Explain how recording constellations over a year reveals a pattern you can predict.
items.answer: The same constellations return in the same seasons each year, so you can predict which will appear

steps: A repeating yearly pattern lets you forecast which stars will be visible in a given season.

items.prompt: A student graphs sunrise times over several months and sees them change smoothly. How does graphing help compared to a list?
items.answer: The graph shows the smooth trend and makes it easy to predict future sunrise times

steps: The graph's shape reveals the repeating trend, supporting predictions.

items.prompt: Two students measure shadows on the same day but at different times and get different lengths. Explain why, using the pattern.
items.answer: The Sun's height changes through the day, so shadow length changes with the time of day

steps: Because shadow length depends on the Sun's height, different times give different lengths.

items.prompt: Use the day-night pattern to explain why it is daytime in one part of the world while it is night in another.
items.answer: Earth's rotation means one side faces the Sun (day) while the other faces away (night)

steps: As Earth spins, only the side facing the Sun has daylight at any moment.
